title: Married priests
hook: Eastern Catholic priests are often married

segments.voice: Yesterday, babies receive everything: in the Eastern churches an infant is baptized, chrismated and given communion in one morning. Your line was all three at once. Did a small child cross your mind? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

Sunday, after the Divine Liturgy, in a parish hall that smells of coffee. The priest is still in his black cassock, and a small boy is tugging at the hem of it, asking for a donut. Not a stranger's boy. His own son. Across the room a woman is pouring coffee and greeting newcomers by name, and people call her by a title of her own. For a Latin Catholic visiting for the first time, it's a double take. A married Catholic priest? With kids? Nobody here is breaking a rule. This is an Eastern Catholic parish, in full communion with Rome, doing what its tradition has long done. Today is about that priest, and about the woman at the coffee urn.
screen: `A PRIEST WITH A SON AT HIS HEM.` → `A WOMAN WITH A TITLE OF HER OWN.` → `NOBODY IS BREAKING A RULE.`

segments.voice: Start with the New Testament, which doesn't hide that the apostles had families. Mark's Gospel says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Simon's wife's mother lay in a fit of a fever," and Jesus heals her. Simon is Peter. Peter had a mother-in-law, so Peter had a wife. And when Paul lists what a bishop should be, he writes that he must be "blameless, the husband of one wife." Next, what the Catechism says about the two disciplines today. In the Latin Church, it says, priests are normally chosen from men who live a celibate life and intend to keep it, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Then it adds that in the Eastern Churches a different discipline has been in force for many centuries: bishops are chosen only from celibates, but married men can be ordained deacons and priests. Both, the Catechism says, are honored. Neither is called second best. Then the order of things, which surprises people. In these churches a man marries first, and then may be ordained. A priest doesn't go looking for a wife after ordination. If a single man is ordained, he stays single. Last, the woman at the coffee urn. Her life is shaped by her husband's calling too: the late phone calls, the shared table, the move to a new parish. Eastern Christians give her a title. Greek speakers call her presbytera. In Arabic-speaking parishes she is khouria. Ukrainians have their own word for her, and so do Russians. Her title is spoken with respect.
screen: `PETER HAD A MOTHER-IN-LAW.` · `TWO DISCIPLINES, BOTH HONORED.` · `MARRY FIRST, THEN ORDINATION.` · `THE PRIEST'S WIFE HAS A TITLE.` · then, large: `BLAMELESS, THE HUSBAND OF ONE WIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a priest's family in mind. It might be a married Eastern priest, or a deacon and his wife in a Latin parish, or a pastor of any church you know who comes home tired to people who love him. Settle, and breathe. Picture their kitchen table on a Sunday night. Who's there? What did the day cost them? Let your attention rest on the one who usually gets thanked least. If you pray, you can simply say, Lord, have mercy, for that household. If you don't, just wish them a quiet evening. The bell holds the time.
Married priests. In the Eastern Catholic churches, married men may be ordained priests, a discipline the Catechism calls long-standing. They marry before ordination, never after. Today's word.
Your line: the priest's wife. Today, notice the person standing just behind someone else's calling, and thank them by name. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: In the Eastern Catholic churches married men may be ordained deacons and priests, provided they marry before ordination; bishops are chosen from celibate clergy. In the Latin Church, priests are normally celibate.

original.note: Greek, as Greek-speaking Christians say it today: the priest's wife.

trapdoor: what you thought: Catholic priests can never be married.
what it means: in the Eastern Catholic churches, married men may be ordained priests; they marry first, and bishops come from the celibate clergy.
what a scholar hears: CCC 1579–1580 sets the Latin discipline of celibacy beside an Eastern discipline it says has been in force for many centuries, and honors both.

notes: CCC 1579–1580 paraphrased: Latin priests normally chosen from celibates; in the Eastern Churches a different discipline has been in force for many centuries, bishops chosen solely from celibates, married men ordainable as deacons and priests; Catechism says this practice is highly esteemed. Confirm 'both are honored' is fair.

Titles for the priest's wife: presbytera (Greek), khouria (Arabic); Ukrainian and Russian titles alluded to but not named (pani-matka / dobrodiyka; matushka). Confirm spellings and usage across Eastern Catholic churches.

Index hook says Eastern priests are 'often married'; the script avoids any proportion. Practice varies by church and country, and some Eastern Catholic churches have historically had restrictions on married priests in some countries. Confirm the framing.
Douay-Rheims wording of Mark 1:30 and 1 Timothy 3:2: confirm.
'Lord, have mercy' offered as an existing prayer (the Kyrie), not a new one.
Original: πρεσβυτέρα and its modern Greek pronunciation; confirm.
